headline: Maine, Vermont regulators prepare hemp sellers for 11 December ban
dek: Regulators in both states issued notices on 17 November: Maine told shops to check stock, while Vermont plans an intrastate market for products the federal ban will cut off.
key_points: Maine's Office of Cannabis Policy and its alcohol bureau told licensees on 17 November that most intoxicating hemp products face a federal ban on 11 December unless Congress acts.
The Maine notice names hemp THC drinks and gummies sold in dispensaries, liquor stores, bars and restaurants, and urges businesses to review inventory and talk to lawyers.
Vermont's Cannabis Control Board said the same day it plans rules for an in-state market for hemp products that meet Vermont's THC limits but lose federal hemp status.
Vermont warned that sellers of those products could face banking, payment, shipping and insurance problems, and Section 280E tax exposure, because state approval does not override federal law.
body: Two New England states have started preparing their hemp markets for 11 December, the date most intoxicating hemp-derived THC products lose federal legality unless Congress changes course. On 17 November Maine's cannabis and alcohol regulators sent businesses a joint warning to check their shelves, and Vermont's Cannabis Control Board said it intends to write rules for an in-state market for products that will no longer qualify as federal hemp.

The two notices show the choice every state now faces with 22 days to go: tell businesses to clear out affected stock, or try to keep some of it legal inside state lines. Neither state can change federal law, and both say so.

The notice came from the Office of Cannabis Policy and the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and Lottery Operations, both in Maine's Department of Administrative and Financial Services, and is listed on the office's guidance page dated 17 November. According to The Marijuana Herald's account of it, the agencies singled out hemp THC beverages, gummies and similar products sold at medical and adult-use dispensaries, liquor stores, bars and restaurants.

The agencies said they had received questions from licensees and registrants. They urged businesses to review inventory, identify products that may be affected and consult a lawyer about existing stock before the deadline. They stressed that the notice describes a change in federal law, not new Maine rules.

Maine's own cannabis programmes are largely outside the problem. Products sold through the state's medical and adult-use systems are not affected by this federal change as long as they contain no hemp-derived cannabinoids, the notice said. Hemp-derived products stocked by licensed cannabis stores are another matter and may still be caught.
> States cannot stop 11 December. They can only decide how much of the shelf to save inside their own borders.

Vermont is going further. In guidance published on 17 November, the Cannabis Control Board said it intends to start rulemaking for an intrastate market covering hemp products that comply with Vermont's existing THC limits but fall outside the new federal definition, The Marijuana Herald reported. The authority comes from Act 178, passed this year, which revived Vermont's State Hemp Program and put licensing of hemp producers, processors and products under the same board that regulates cannabis.

The board set no start date. It said rulemaking would begin once federal THC thresholds are clear enough, and any market would stay inside Vermont's current limits on intoxicating hemp. Under existing Vermont rules, products above certain THC levels or marketed mainly for intoxication are already treated as cannabis, not hemp. By our reading, that makes the plan narrower than it sounds: it would mostly matter for lower-strength items that fit Vermont's limits but exceed the federal 0.4 milligram per-container cap, a group The Marijuana Herald said could include some full-spectrum CBD products.

The board was blunt about the risks. Businesses selling products excluded from federal hemp status could struggle to get banking, card processing, shipping and insurance, it said, and could become subject to Section 280E, the tax rule that bars ordinary deductions for trafficking in Schedule I or II substances.

From 11 December, federal hemp is defined by total THC, including THCA, of 0.3% or less on a dry-weight basis, and finished products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container count as marijuana, MJBizDaily reported. A narrower first step took effect on 12 November, banning products with cannabinoids the plant cannot make naturally, such as fully synthetic ones. MJBizDaily counted Illinois and Missouri as joining roughly 16 other states that limit hemp THC sales to licensed cannabis stores.

Congress still has options. As we reported on 18 November, Sens. Tim Sheehy and Amy Klobuchar have a draft bill that would replace the per-container cap with a 1% total THC limit and FDA oversight. Any fix would most likely ride on the funding bill due by the same date.

For Maine bars, restaurants and liquor stores, the notice is a practical deadline to decide what to do with hemp drinks and edibles already in stock. For Vermont hemp makers, the board's plan offers a possible lifeline, but one that would carry the same federal handicaps cannabis companies live with: no easy banking and a heavy federal tax bill. For multistate brands, a patchwork of in-state markets would mean separate products, labels and supply chains for each state that builds one.

Watch Congress and the stopgap funding bill before 11 December. Watch for Vermont's draft rules and whether other states copy its intrastate approach. In Illinois, a federal judge was set to hear a challenge to the state's hemp law on 19 November, according to MJBizDaily; a ruling there would be the next signal on how far states can go.
